body:
Common salt is more than a food ingredient

Common salt is sodium chloride, NaCl. It is used to season and preserve food and is an important raw material for several other chemicals. It can be recovered from seawater and other brines by evaporation, or obtained from rock-salt deposits. An aqueous solution of pure NaCl is approximately neutral, because NaCl is the salt of a strong acid, HCl, and a strong base, NaOH.

Salt production gives this chemical a genuine Gujarat connection. Salt pans in Kachchh and along the Gujarat coast recover salt from brine. The Government of India's One District One Product listing identifies salt as a product of Kachchh; this is a location example, not a special type of chemical salt.

The chlor-alkali process

A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride is called brine. When electricity passes through brine, sodium hydroxide (NaOH), chlorine (Cl2) and hydrogen (H2) are produced. This school-level reaction is called the chlor-alkali process:

2NaCl + 2H2O → 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2

Chlorine is released at the positive electrode (anode), hydrogen at the negative electrode (cathode), and sodium hydroxide solution forms near the cathode. Sodium hydroxide is an important strong alkali used in soap, detergent and paper manufacture.

Bleaching powder: preparation, notation and uses

Bleaching powder is produced when chlorine reacts with dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)2. In the NCERT Class 10 Science reprint available in 2026, it is represented by Ca(ClO)2, while the actual commercial composition is more complex. The textbook expresses the reaction as:

2Ca(OH)2 + 2Cl2 → Ca(ClO)2 + CaCl2 + 2H2O

Bleaching powder is used to bleach cotton, linen and wood pulp; as an oxidising agent; and for disinfecting drinking water. It is not the same substance as common salt, NaCl, even though chlorine derived from brine is used in its preparation.

Two textbook notations

Earlier NCERT editions represented bleaching powder as CaOCl2 (calcium oxychloride), while NCERT's 2026–27 reprint uses Ca(ClO)2 and explicitly notes that commercial bleaching powder is a complex mixture. Recognise both school-book conventions when reading questions; neither is a complete description of every commercial sample.

Prelims focus

  • Common salt: sodium chloride, NaCl; its aqueous solution is approximately neutral.
  • Brine is a concentrated aqueous NaCl solution.
  • Chlor-alkali process: NaOH, Cl2 and H2 are produced.
  • Chlorine forms at the anode; hydrogen forms at the cathode.
  • Chlorine reacts with dry slaked lime to give bleaching powder.
  • Trap: Bleaching powder and baking soda have different compositions and uses.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, section 2.4.3, pp. 29–31, 2026–27 reprint (consulted 3 November 2026); NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 2, p. 30, earlier edition, reprinted October 2013 (for CaOCl2 notation); Government of India, National Portal, ODOP, “Salt—Kachchh, Gujarat,” updated 11 September 2026, consulted 3 November 2026; Office of the Salt Commissioner, “Salt Industry in India,” “Major Salt Producing Centres.”]

body:
Baking soda: a mild basic salt

Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3 (also called sodium bicarbonate). Its aqueous solution is mildly basic. It is used in some antacids and in the preparation of baking powder. Baking powder is not pure baking soda: it combines baking soda with a weak edible acid, commonly tartaric acid. Carbon dioxide released when moisture or heat allows them to react helps cakes and bread rise.

On heating, sodium hydrogencarbonate forms sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide:

2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 (on heating)

Baking soda also has a traditional application in soda-acid fire extinguishers; the gas released from its reaction with an acid is carbon dioxide.

Washing soda: hydrated sodium carbonate

Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O. Sodium carbonate can be obtained from baking soda, and crystallisation with water gives the hydrated salt called washing soda. Its solution is basic. It is used as a domestic cleaning agent, in glass, soap and paper industries, and to remove permanent hardness of water.

The 10H2O means that each formula unit of the crystalline salt contains a fixed ratio of 10 water molecules as water of crystallisation. It does not mean that the crystals are merely wet on the outside.

Plaster of Paris and gypsum

Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO4·2H2O. Controlled heating at about 373 K (100°C) removes part of its water of crystallisation to produce Plaster of Paris (POP), calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO4·(1/2)H2O.

When POP is mixed with water it sets into a hard mass by converting back to gypsum. For each formula unit of POP, approximately 1.5 additional water molecules are needed to regain the 2-water gypsum composition. POP is used for casts supporting fractured bones, moulded objects and smooth decorative surfaces. Because it reacts with moisture and hardens, POP must be stored in a moisture-resistant container.

Do not confuse these names

Common nameFormulaKey use or fact
Baking sodaNaHCO3Baking powder and antacids
Washing sodaNa2CO3·10H2OCleaning and water softening
GypsumCaSO4·2H2OSource of POP
Plaster of ParisCaSO4·(1/2)H2OHard-setting casts and moulds

Prelims focus

  • Baking soda: NaHCO3; baking powder also contains an edible acid such as tartaric acid.
  • Heating baking soda releases CO2 and produces Na2CO3.
  • Washing soda: Na2CO3·10H2O; it helps remove permanent water hardness.
  • Gypsum: CaSO4·2H2O; POP: CaSO4·(1/2)H2O.
  • POP sets by taking up water and converting back to gypsum.
  • Trap: The water in hydrated washing soda is part of its crystal composition, not surface moisture.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, sections 2.4.3–2.4.4, pp. 31–33, including “Baking Soda,” “Washing Soda” and “Plaster of Paris” (consulted 3 November 2026); NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 2, pp. 31–33, earlier edition.]

body:
What a solution tells us

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of 2 or more substances: its composition is uniform throughout at the particle level. In an aqueous solution of common salt, water is the solvent and dissolved sodium chloride is the solute. A solution may be dilute or concentrated depending on the relative amount of solute. At a given temperature, a saturated solution contains as much dissolved solute as it can hold under those conditions.

The term solution describes the physical uniformity of a mixture, not whether it is acidic, basic or neutral. Dilute hydrochloric acid is an acidic aqueous solution, sodium hydroxide solution is basic, and pure sodium chloride solution is approximately neutral.

True solutions, colloids and suspensions

A colloid contains finely dispersed particles that are too small to see individually with the unaided eye. It may look uniform, but it is a heterogeneous mixture. In an emulsion such as milk, small droplets of one liquid are dispersed in another. A suspension, such as coarse mud in water, has larger suspended particles that may settle when left undisturbed.

PropertyTrue solutionColloidSuspension
NatureHomogeneousHeterogeneousHeterogeneous
ExampleSalt in waterMilkCoarse mud in water
Light pathNot visible by scatteringCan be visibleCan be visible
On standingDoes not settleUsually does not settleOften settles
Ordinary filtrationDoes not remove soluteDoes not remove particlesCan remove particles

The Tyndall effect

Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light so that its path becomes visible under suitable conditions. This is the Tyndall effect. A salt-water true solution does not ordinarily show a visible light path, while diluted milk usually does. A suspension also scatters light, but its larger particles can settle. Therefore light scattering alone does not prove that a mixture is a colloid; settling behaviour also matters.

Link with acids, bases and salts

Indicators and pH are used to investigate the acid-base character of an aqueous sample. They do not themselves tell us whether the sample is a true solution or a colloid. Similarly, dissolving a salt in water does not guarantee a neutral pH: sodium chloride solution is ordinarily neutral, whereas aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate and sodium carbonate are basic.

Prelims focus

  • Solute: dissolved component; solvent: the component that dissolves it.
  • A true solution is homogeneous; a colloid is heterogeneous although it may look uniform.
  • The Tyndall effect is light scattering by colloidal particles.
  • Suspension particles can settle and can often be separated by ordinary filtration.
  • NaCl solution is approximately neutral; NaHCO3 solution is mildly basic.
  • Trap: A transparent solution is not necessarily neutral, and a light-scattering mixture is not necessarily a stable colloid.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 2, “Is Matter Around Us Pure?”, sections 2.1–2.2.3, pp. 14–18, 2018–19 printing; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 2, pp. 14–18, as reproduced in the Class 9 science volume; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, sections 2.2–2.4, pp. 22–33 (consulted 3 November 2026).]
